content_html:
Spatial–Conceptual Mapping

Rooms & Colours

Even when we think “purely conceptually,” the brain recruits systems used for vision, space, and action to build internal models. Mapping ideas into rooms (spatial compartments) and colours (affective/salience tags) creates distinct contexts that reduce interference, strengthen retrieval cues, and provide a felt sense of structure.

Rooms act as contextual “namespaces.” Coloured clusters are idea-attractors; dashed paths indicate narrative or proof flow across compartments.

How to build a “rooms & colours” system

Define rooms by function. e.g., Room A = axioms/definitions; Room B = lemmas; Room C = counterexamples/edge cases.

Assign stable colours. Use colours as semantic/affective tags (e.g., red = constraints, blue = generality, green = constructive steps, yellow = open questions).

Create entry cues. A consistent doorway (a phrase, icon, or breath cue) helps re-enter a room quickly.

Place idea-attractors. Add 3–5 key “nodes” per room (core ideas); link them with intended flows (proof routes, dependencies).

Use boundary resets. Deliberately step into a different room to reduce interference when stuck.

Version the map. Keep a light “changelog” (v1 → v2) to avoid brittle overfitting to early metaphors.

Neuroscience & cognition

Abstract concepts piggyback on image schemas (path, container, balance); conceptual metaphors recruit perceptual & motor circuits for structure. “Rooms” behave like event boundaries that prevent memory interference, they provide distinct retrieval cues via spatial & colour contexts. Repeated rehearsal stabilises clusters (attractor-like representations) and colours add affective salience to boost consolidation & recall.
